name: Temi Tea Garden
tagline: Sikkim's own tea estate, planted under the last Chogyal in 1969
meta_description: Temi Tea Garden, South Sikkim: the 1969 royal estate, free tea walks, factory visits, November cherry blossom, Cherry Resort and 2026 costs.
summary: Temi Tea Garden is Sikkim's main tea estate, about 177 ha of terraces below Tendong hill in South Sikkim, ≈ 16–20 km from both Namchi and Ravangla. It was set up in 1969 under the last Chogyal and is now run by the state. Walking the garden roads is free; come for half a day or one night.
intro: Temi Tea Garden spreads over about 177 ha, roughly 440 acres, of slopes running down from the Tendong hill range in South Sikkim. Tea bushes cover the hill in neat rows at around 1,500 m, with shade trees, a factory and small workers' villages along the road. It lies ≈ 16–20 km from Namchi and from Ravangla, about 45 minutes to an hour from each, which makes it an easy half-day trip from either town.

The estate was set up in 1969 under Palden Thondup Namgyal, the 12th and last Chogyal of Sikkim, and it belongs today to the Government of Sikkim, which runs it through its tea board. Production is about 100 tonnes a year, and the garden switched to organic farming from 2005. Most Sikkim tea in the shops is sold simply as 'Temi tea', under brand names such as Sikkim Solja, Mystique and Kanchanjunga Tea.

For travellers the appeal is simple. The estate roads are quiet, the walking is free, and on a clear autumn morning you look across tea terraces to the snow peaks. In November the Himalayan cherry trees along the approach turn pink. Visitors can usually see the factory by asking at the office. Stay at Cherry Resort inside the estate for a night, or come from Ravangla or Namchi for the morning and buy tea at source before you leave.

story.title: A king's tea garden on the Tendong slopes
paras: Temi began in 1969, when Sikkim was still a kingdom under Palden Thondup Namgyal, its 12th and last Chogyal. Wikipedia's article on Sikkim tea says he set the garden up as a source of jobs for the large number of Tibetan refugees then living in the region. Part of the land had once held early-20th-century missionary buildings, which the Sikkim government had acquired in 1954. Tea went in on the gentle, loamy slopes below Tendong hill.

Six years later, after the referendum of April 1975, Sikkim joined India as a state and the monarchy ended. The garden carried on and is today owned by the Government of Sikkim and run through its tea board. It now covers about 177 ha and makes around 100 tonnes of tea a year. About three-quarters goes to the Kolkata auctions and the rest is packed for the home market. Temi won the All India Quality Award in 1994 and 1995.

Temi began converting to organic production in 2005, and Sikkim tea has been certified organic by the Institute for Market Ecology. Unlike Darjeeling, Sikkim tea has no geographical indication tag yet, though efforts are under way. The seasons show in the cup: first flush in spring is light, golden and floral, the monsoon flush fuller and mellow, the autumn flush rounded with a hint of spice. Buy a packet from each season and taste the difference at home.
story.source: Wikipedia: 'Temi Tea Garden', 'Sikkim tea', 'Palden Thondup Namgyal'

did_you_know: Temi Tea Garden won the All India Quality Award for tea in 1994 and again in 1995.
About three-quarters of Temi's tea is sold through the Kolkata auctions, and the rest is packed for sale in India.
Temi tea is sold under several names, including Sikkim Solja, Mystique and Kanchanjunga Tea.
facts: Organic Temi tea, cherry blossom, Tendong views

highlights.title: Free walks on the estate roads
highlights.text: The roads that wind through Temi's 177 ha are open to walkers and cost nothing. Start near the factory and walk downhill between the rows, watching pluckers at work in season. An hour gives you the feel of the place; two hours takes you deep into the terraces.

highlights.title: Tea made where it grows
highlights.text: Temi makes about 100 tonnes of organic tea a year. Visitors can usually see the factory by asking at the office, and packets are sold near it. Buying at source is the surest way to get genuine Temi tea, and a good gift to carry home.

highlights.title: Cherry blossom in November
highlights.text: Himalayan cherry trees line the approach to Temi and flower from November, when the pink blossom sits against green tea and, on clear days, the snow peaks. It is also one of the driest, clearest months of the year here, so it is our favourite time to visit.

highlights.title: A night at Cherry Resort
highlights.text: Cherry Resort, inside the estate, is a government building, once the Yatri Niwas, now run privately on lease. Staying overnight lets you walk the garden at dawn, before day-trippers arrive, and watch evening light on Tendong hill above the terraces.

highlights.title: A royal story in a cup
highlights.text: The garden was started in 1969 under Palden Thondup Namgyal, Sikkim's last Chogyal, partly to give work to Tibetan refugees. Knowing that history, and tasting first, monsoon and autumn flush side by side, turns a pleasant stop into a lesson in Sikkim's recent past.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps link Siliguri with Namchi for about ₹300–400 a seat and with Ravangla for ₹350–450, indicative, 2026. Few shared jeeps run into the estate itself. Ask at the Namchi or Ravangla stand whether one is going via Temi; seats are few and mostly morning. Otherwise take a local taxi for the last stretch, and check current status before you travel.

Most people come by taxi from Namchi or Ravangla, ≈ 16–20 km and 45 minutes to an hour each way. A local taxi with waiting costs about ₹1,500–2,500 return, indicative, 2026. From Siliguri, a small car or SUV costs about the same as the ₹4,500–6,000 Siliguri–Ravangla run.

New Jalpaiguri (NJP) is the nearest major station, about 4 hours away by road. Take a shared jeep from the Siliguri stands to Namchi or Ravangla and continue by local taxi, or book a car from the station.
Bagdogra (IXB) is ≈ 120 km away and has the most flights. Pakyong airport near Gangtok has had irregular flights, so check current status before you travel and plan around Bagdogra.

where_to_stay: The only place to sleep inside the estate is Cherry Resort, a government building that was once the Yatri Niwas and is now privately run on lease. It is named after the Himalayan cherry trees on the approach, which flower from November, and it gives you the tea terraces at dawn and dusk without day-trip crowds. Rooms are limited, so book well ahead for November and the October holidays. For more choice, base yourself in Ravangla, where Mt. Narsing Village Resort and the simple hotels on Kewzing Road suit most budgets, or in Namchi's market area. Homestays in nearby villages are another low-cost option.
costs: Local taxi Namchi or Ravangla → Temi, return
budget_tip: Walking the estate roads is free, so skip paid tours, share a local taxi from Namchi or Ravangla with other travellers and buy your tea at the estate rather than in Gangtok shops.
tips: Come in the morning; mist and cloud often roll up the slopes after noon, especially from April onwards.
Stay on the estate roads and paths and do not walk between the bushes or pick leaves.
Ask before photographing pluckers at work, and do not hold them up during their shift.
Plucking pauses in the dormant winter months, so visit from March to November to see the garden at work.
Wear shoes with grip; the estate roads are steep in places and slippery after rain.

experiences.title: Morning walk through the Temi tea terraces
experiences.summary: Walk the quiet roads of Sikkim's main tea estate, about 177 ha of terraces below Tendong hill. In season you see pluckers at work, and on clear mornings the snow peaks rise beyond the rows. It costs nothing and suits all ages if you keep to the gentler loops.
body: Temi's estate roads loop down and across the hillside through about 177 ha of tea. Start near the factory and walk downhill between the rows of clipped bushes, with tall shade trees overhead and small workers' villages along the way. The slopes are gentle by Himalayan standards, which is why the garden was laid out here, below the Tendong range, in 1969. Wikipedia describes the soil as loamy, on slopes of about 30–50 per cent, which drains well in the heavy monsoon rain.

From March to November, pluckers work the rows with baskets on their backs, picking the top two leaves and a bud. Spring's first flush is the most prized, but every season has its own leaf and smell. On a clear morning, especially in October and November, the snow peaks show to the north across the terraces. Birds are busy in the shade trees, and the only traffic is the odd tea lorry or estate jeep.

The walk is free. Keep to the roads and marked paths, do not cut between bushes or pick leaves, and ask before photographing workers. An hour is enough for a short loop, two hours for a longer one; walking back uphill takes more time than you think, so arrange for your taxi to meet you lower down. Carry water and sun protection, as there is little shade on the open roads.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for Temi Tea Garden
faqs.a: No. Walking the estate roads at Temi Tea Garden is free. You pay only for transport and anything you buy, such as packets of tea. Keep to the roads and paths and respect the workers' areas. Arrangements can change, so check current status before you travel, especially for factory access.

faqs.q: How long should I spend at Temi Tea Garden
faqs.a: Two to three hours is enough for a walk through the terraces, a look at the factory if it is open to visitors that day, and buying tea. If you stay the night at Cherry Resort, you can walk at dawn and dusk too. Most people combine Temi with Namchi or Ravangla in one day.

faqs.q: When is the best time to see tea plucking at Temi
faqs.a: Plucking runs from about March to November. March and April bring the first flush, the most prized spring tea, and October and November bring the autumn flush along with the clearest mountain views. In the dormant winter months, bushes are pruned and there is little plucking to see.

experiences.title: Factory visit and buying Temi tea at source
experiences.cost: Free or a small fee; ask at the factory office
experiences.summary: Temi's factory turns fresh leaf into black and other teas, and the estate is promoted as a place where visitors can see production. Ask at the office for a look inside, then buy packets of organic Temi tea at source, choosing by season and grade.
body: Temi makes about 100 tonnes of tea a year, most of it black tea, with smaller amounts of other styles. Wikipedia notes that the estate is being promoted for tourism, with visitors getting the chance to see the production facility. In practice, access depends on the day, the season and the manager's permission, so ask politely at the factory office when you arrive. Mornings on working days are your best chance.

If you get in, you will see the main steps of orthodox tea making: withering the leaf, rolling it, letting it oxidise and drying it, before sorting by grade. The smell of drying leaf is the thing most visitors remember. Do not touch machines, keep children close and follow any rules on photos. In the off months, or on Sundays and holidays, the floor may be quiet or closed. A short visit of 20–30 minutes is usual, and a thank-you to the staff who show you round is always welcome.

Packets of Temi tea are usually sold near the factory, under brand names such as Sikkim Solja, Mystique and Kanchanjunga Tea. Buying here supports the estate and guarantees what you get. Ask which flush each packet comes from: spring first flush is light and floral, monsoon fuller, autumn rounded. Prices vary by grade and change often, so check current status before you travel. Tea keeps best in a sealed tin away from light, so pack it carefully for the journey home and drink the first flush within a few months.

faqs.q: Can tourists visit the Temi tea factory
faqs.a: Often, yes, but it is not guaranteed. The estate is promoted for tourism and visitors can see production, but access depends on the day, the season and permission from the office. Ask politely at the factory office on arrival, preferably on a weekday morning between March and November, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where can I buy genuine Temi tea
faqs.a: The surest place is the estate itself, where packets are usually sold near the factory under names such as Sikkim Solja, Mystique and Kanchanjunga Tea. Government outlets and shops in Gangtok and Namchi also stock it. At the estate you can ask which season and grade each packet comes from.

faqs.q: Is Temi tea organic
faqs.a: Yes. Temi began converting to organic production in 2005, and Sikkim tea has been certified organic by the Institute for Market Ecology. Sikkim as a whole is known for organic farming. Unlike Darjeeling tea, Sikkim tea does not yet have a geographical indication tag, though efforts are under way.

experiences.title: Himalayan cherry blossom in November
experiences.summary: In November the Himalayan cherry trees along the road into Temi flower pink, just as the tea terraces are still green and the skies are at their clearest. Combine a slow walk under the blossom with the tea garden and, on a good day, a view of the snow peaks.
body: Unlike Japanese cherries, which bloom in spring, the Himalayan cherry flowers in autumn and early winter. At Temi, the trees that line the approach to the estate come into flower from November, and the resort inside the garden takes its name from them. The pink blossom against dark green tea is the picture most people come for, and it is worth getting up early to see it in soft light.

November is also one of the best months for weather here. The monsoon has gone, the air is dry and the morning views of the snow peaks are often clear. The autumn flush is finishing in the garden, so you may still see pluckers at work. Days are mild in the sun and cool in the shade; evenings are cold enough for a jacket. Rooms in the area fill early for the October holidays and November weekends, so plan ahead.

Exact flowering time shifts by a week or two each year with the weather, so check current status before you travel. Book Cherry Resort or a room in Ravangla or Namchi early for November weekends. Walking under the trees is free. Please do not break branches or pull blossoms for photos, and park only where the road is wide enough for tea lorries to pass. If the trees near the road are crowded, walk a little further along the estate road, where you often have the blossom to yourself.

faqs.q: When do cherry blossoms bloom in Sikkim
faqs.a: The Himalayan cherry in Sikkim flowers in autumn and early winter, not spring. At Temi Tea Garden the trees along the approach usually bloom from November. The exact week shifts with the weather each year, so check current status before you travel and plan a flexible day in Ravangla or Namchi.

faqs.q: Is November a good time to visit Temi Tea Garden
faqs.a: Yes, it is one of the best. The monsoon is over, skies are often clear for the snow peaks, the autumn flush is finishing and the cherry trees are in flower. It is also the busiest month, so book rooms early and arrive in the morning for quieter roads and better light.

faqs.q: Do I need to pay to see the cherry blossom at Temi
faqs.a: No. The cherry trees line the public approach and estate roads, and walking under them is free. You pay only for transport and any tea you buy. Please do not break branches or pick blossoms, and park only where tea lorries and estate vehicles can still pass.

experiences.title: Slow walk on the estate road below Tendong
experiences.summary: Walk the upper estate roads at Temi with Tendong hill, sacred to the Lepcha, rising above the terraces. It is an easy, free half morning for birds, views and village life, and a gentle alternative for anyone who cannot manage the full Tendong hike from Damthang.
body: Temi's tea is planted on the slopes of the Tendong hill range, and the long forested ridge of Tendong rises above the upper part of the estate. Lepcha tradition holds that their ancestors survived a great flood on top of Tendong, and every 8 August Tendong Lho Rumfaat, a Sikkim state holiday, gives thanks to the hill. From Temi you get to look up at it without climbing it, which suits seniors, young children and anyone short of time or breath.

Pick an upper estate road and walk slowly along the contour, with tea below and forest above. On clear mornings the snow peaks show to the north. Shade trees and forest edges are good for birds, so carry binoculars if you have them. You will pass small homes where workers' families live; a greeting in Nepali, namaste, goes a long way. Two to three hours at an easy pace is plenty.

The walk is free and needs no guide if you keep to the estate roads. Turn back the way you came if you are unsure of a junction, and arrange your taxi pickup point in advance. If you want to climb Tendong itself, hire a local guide for the forest trail from Damthang. From June to September expect leeches, slippery roads and cloud, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I see Tendong hill from Temi Tea Garden
faqs.a: Yes. Temi's terraces run down from the Tendong hill range, so the long forested ridge rises above the upper estate. You see it best on clear mornings from October to December. To climb to the top, go to Damthang on the Namchi–Ravangla road and hire a local guide for the forest trail.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide to walk around Temi
faqs.a: No, not for the estate roads. They are easy to follow, and the walk is free. Arrange a pickup point with your taxi, turn back if you are unsure of a junction and keep out of the tea rows. For the Tendong hill hike from Damthang, a local guide is a good idea.

faqs.q: Is Temi good for birdwatching
faqs.a: It can be pleasant for casual birding. The shade trees in the garden and the forest edges on the upper slopes attract common hill birds, and mornings are most active. Serious birders usually head to the Maenam forest above Ravangla, but a slow walk at Temi with binoculars is a good warm-up.

faqs.q: Is Temi Tea Garden worth visiting
faqs.a: Yes, especially from Ravangla or Namchi. It is Sikkim's best-known tea estate, set up in 1969 under the last Chogyal, and walking its roads is free. You get quiet terraces, a chance to see the factory, genuine Temi tea at source and, on clear mornings, snow peaks. Half a day is enough for most people.

faqs.q: How do I reach Temi Tea Garden from Gangtok
faqs.a: Most people come via Ravangla or Namchi. A shared jeep from Gangtok to Ravangla costs about ₹250–350 a seat, indicative for 2026, then a local taxi covers the ≈ 16–20 km to Temi. A reserved car from Gangtok can do Temi and Ravangla in a long day. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Temi Tea Garden from Namchi and Ravangla
faqs.a: Temi is ≈ 16–20 km from Namchi and about the same from Ravangla, roughly 45 minutes to an hour by road from each. A local taxi with waiting costs about ₹1,500–2,500 return, indicative for 2026. Few shared jeeps go into the estate, so a taxi is the easy choice.

faqs.q: Can I stay inside Temi Tea Garden
faqs.a: Yes. Cherry Resort sits inside the estate in a government building that was once the Yatri Niwas and is now privately run on lease. Rooms are limited, so book early, especially for November and the October holidays. Otherwise stay in Ravangla or Namchi and visit for the day.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Temi Tea Garden
faqs.a: March to May for the first flush and spring green, and October to November for clear mountain views and, in November, cherry blossom. June to September brings rain, cloud and leeches, though the garden is very green. In the dormant winter months the bushes are pruned and there is little plucking to see.

faqs.q: Who owns Temi Tea Garden
faqs.a: The Government of Sikkim owns Temi Tea Garden and runs it through its tea board. The estate was set up in 1969 under Palden Thondup Namgyal, the last Chogyal, before Sikkim joined India in 1975. It covers about 177 ha and makes around 100 tonnes of tea a year.

faqs.q: Is Temi tea better than Darjeeling tea
faqs.a: It is different rather than better or worse. Temi grows at similar heights and makes organic orthodox tea with light, floral first flushes and fuller monsoon teas. Darjeeling has a much longer history, many more estates and a geographical indication tag, which Sikkim tea does not have yet. Try both and decide.

faqs.q: Is Temi Tea Garden good for a honeymoon
faqs.a: Yes, for a quiet night or two. Cherry Resort inside the estate gives you early walks through empty terraces, sunsets over the hills and, in November, cherry blossom. There is little nightlife or shopping, so pair it with Pelling or Gangtok if you want more going on.

faqs.q: Do foreigners need a permit to visit Temi
faqs.a: Foreign nationals need Sikkim's Restricted Area Permit, which is free and valid for 30 days. Apply online through e-FRRO or get it at the Melli or Rangpo checkposts on the way in. Indian nationals need only photo ID. No separate permit is needed for the tea garden. Check current status before you travel.
